'''''Helleborus niger''''', commonly called '''Christmas rose''' or '''black hellebore''', is an [[evergreen]] [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[flowering plant]] in the buttercup family, [[Ranunculaceae]]. It is one of about 20 species from the genus ''[[Helleborus]]''.
It is a poisonous [[cottage garden]] favourite because it flowers in the depths of winter.

Although the flowers resemble [[dog rose|wild roses]] (and despite its common name), Christmas rose does not belong to the [[rose]] family ([[Rosaceae]]).

==Taxonomy==
The black hellebore was described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in volume one of his ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' in 1753.<ref>{{cite book | last=Linnaeus | first=Carolus | title=Species Plantarum| volume=1 | publisher=Laurentii Salvii |location=Stockholm | year=1753|chapter= Tomus I | chapter-url=https://biodiversitylibrary.org/page/358577| page=558|language=la}}</ref> The Latin specific name ''niger'' (black) may refer to the colour of the roots.<ref name="RHSD">
{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/education-learning/blogs/libraries/December-2016/hellebores|last=Briggs|first = Gill|title=The dark side of the Christmas Rose|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|accessdate=2017-12-26}}</ref> There are two subspecies: ''H. niger'' subsp. ''niger'' and ''H. niger'' subsp. ''macranthus'', which has larger flowers (up to 3.75 in/9 cm across). In the wild, ''H. niger'' subsp. ''niger''  is generally found in mountainous areas in [[Switzerland]], southern [[Germany]], [[Austria]], [[Slovenia]], [[Croatia]] and northern [[Italy]]. ''Helleborus niger'' subsp. ''macranthus'' is found only in northern Italy and adjoining parts of Slovenia.<ref name=GardenersGuide/>

==Description==
''Helleborus niger'' is an [[evergreen]] plant with dark leathery [[pedate]] [[leaf|leaves]] carried on stems 9–12 in (23–30 cm) tall. The large flat flowers, borne on short stems from midwinter to early spring, are generally white, but occasionally with a pink tinge.<ref name=GardenersGuide>Rice, Graham  & Strangman, Elizabeth, ''The Gardener's Guide to Growing Hellebores'', David & Charles/Timber Press (1993) {{ISBN|0-7153-9973-X}}</ref> The tips of the petals may be flushed pink or green, and there is a prominent central boss of yellow. [[File:No. 6., Heleborus niger, by Helga von Cramm, chromolithograph, & prayer by Y.E.T., c. 1880.jpg|thumbnail|''Heleborus niger'', by [[Helga von Cramm]], chromolithograh, with a prayer by Y.E.T., c. 1880.]][[File:Christmas Rose (2023-12-28).JPG|thumb|Christmas rose in a garden]][[File:Helleborus_(three_stages).jpg|thumb|Flowers in two different stages, and fruits]]

[[File:Helleborus_niger_volunteer_seedling_02.JPG|thumb|left|[[Volunteer (botany)|Volunteer seedling]] between paving stones]]

==Distribution==
The natural distribution stretches from the eastern [[Northern Alps (Europe)|northern Alps]] (including the [[Julian Alps]], [[Triglav]]) and [[Southern Alps (Europe)|southern Alps]], west to [[Vorarlberg]]. In addition, ''Helleborus niger'' is common in the [[Apennines]] and northern [[Dinaric Alps]] of Slovenia and Croatia. It has been observed up to an elevation of 1900 meters.<ref name="Finkenzeller">Xaver Finkenzeller: ''Alpenblumen.'' Munich 2003, ISBN 3-576-11482-3. </ref> In the [[Berchtesgaden Alps]], it grow up to an elevation of 1560 meters. In [[Germany]], ''Helleborus niger'' is only native to [[Bavaria]] and in the [[Allgäu Alps]] ''Helleborus niger'' is not [[Native species|indigenous]].<ref name="Dörr-Lippert">Erhard Dörr, Wolfgang Lippert: ''Flora des Allgäus und seiner Umgebung.'' volume 1, IHW-Verlag, Eching bei München, 2001, ISBN 3-930167-50-6, S. 518.</ref>

==Horticulture==
The plant is a traditional [[cottage garden]] favourite because it flowers in the depths of winter. Large-flowered [[cultivar]]s are available, as are pink-flowered and [[double-flowered]] selections. It has been awarded an [[Award of Garden Merit]] (AGM) H4 (hardy throughout the [[British Isles]]) by the [[Royal Horticultural Society]], as has one of its hybrids (see below).<ref name=PlantFinder>''RHS Plant Finder 2009–2010'', p349, Dorling Kindersley, London, 2009, {{ISBN|978-1-4053-4176-9}}</ref>

It can be difficult to grow well; [[Soil pH|acidic soil]] is unsuitable, as are poor, dry conditions and full sun. Moist, [[humus]]-rich, [[Alkali soils|alkaline soil]] in dappled shade is preferable. Leaf-mould can be dug in to improve heavy clay or light sandy soils; lime can be added to 'sweeten' acid soils.<ref name=GardenersGuide/>

===Cultivars===
Since the 1950s, 'Potter's Wheel' has been one of the most famous names associated with ''H. niger''. It originated with a self-sown seedling given by Major [[G. H. Tristram]] of [[Dallington, East Sussex|Dallington]], Sussex, to [[Hilda Davenport-Jones]] who had a nursery at nearby [[Washfield]], Kent.  The seedling proved to be exceptionally large-flowered, but it was too slow-growing to be 'bulked up' quickly, so she propagated it as a rigorously-selected uniform seed strain rather than as a vegetatively propagated [[cultivar]].<ref name=GardenersGuide/>
* 'Potter's Wheel'
* 'Marion' (double-flowered; there are also other unnamed double selections)
* 'Praecox' (early flowering)<ref name=PlantFinder/>

===Hybrids===
Nurserymen have tried for many years to cross ''H. niger'' with oriental hellebores (Lenten roses) ''H.'' × ''hybridus'' to increase the colour range available. Possible hybrids have been announced in the past, only to be disproved, but two crosses have been confirmed in recent years. 'Snow Queen', a white-flowered plant, arose spontaneously in Japan in the late 1990s, but does not look dramatically different from a good ''H. niger''. Raised in 2000 by plant breeder David Tristram (whose father gave the first 'Potter's Wheel' to Washfield Nursery), ''Helleborus'' 'Walberton's Rosemary' is pink-flowered, extremely [[floriferous]], and seems to be intermediate between its parents in many other characteristics.<ref>[http://mygarden.rhs.org.uk/blogs/graham_rice/archive/2008/08/30/the-holy-grail-of-hellebores.aspx The Holy Grail of hellebores] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090912235154/http://mygarden.rhs.org.uk/blogs/graham_rice/archive/2008/08/30/the-holy-grail-of-hellebores.aspx |date=12 September 2009 }} Garden writer and journalist Graham Rice's blog</ref>

''Helleborus niger'' has proved easier to cross with other hellebore species. Crosses between it and ''[[Helleborus argutifolius|H. argutifolius]]'' (formerly known as ''H. corsicus'') are called '''''H.''''' × '''''nigercors'''''. First made in 1931, the hybrid is a large, tough plant with white flowers flushed with green; they are said to be the best of all hellebores for [[cut flowers]].<ref name=GardenersGuide/> It has been awarded an [[Award of Garden Merit|AGM]] H4.<ref name=PlantFinder/> Double-flowered plants are available.<ref name=PlantFinder/>

Hybrids between ''H. niger'' and ''H.'' × ''sternii'' (itself a hybrid, between ''H. argutifolius'' and ''[[Helleborus lividus|H. lividus]]'') were originally called ''H.'' × ''nigristern'', but this name has been changed in favour of '''''H.''''' × '''''ericsmithii''''' (commemorating the [[plantsman]] who made the cross in the 1960s and introduced it in 1972, through The Plantsmen nursery). At their best, the hybrids combine the hardiness of ''H. niger'' and ''H. argutifolius'', the large flowers of ''H. niger'', and the leaf and flower colour of ''H. lividus''.<ref name=GardenersGuide/> Cultivars such as 'Bob's Best', 'HGC Silvermoon', 'Ruby Glow' and 'Winter Moonbeam' are available.<ref name=PlantFinder/>

''Helleborus niger'' has also been crossed with ''H. lividus''; the hybrid was known informally as ''H.'' × ''nigriliv'', but its correct name is '''''H.''''' × '''''ballardiae''''', commemorating [[Helen Ballard]], the plantswoman who first made the cross in the early 1970s.<ref name=GardenersGuide/>

==Poisonous constituents==
All parts of the Christmas Rose plant are considered toxic upon consumption or physical contact with sap from damaged plant tissues. This is due to the fact that its [[organs]] contain varying levels of different [[glycosides]] - which are common plant defense mechanisms against herbivores and microorganisms.<ref name="Cornell">{{cite web |title=Helleborus niger - Christmas Rose |url=https://poisonousplants.ansci.cornell.edu/christmasrose/christmasrose.html |website=Plants poisonous to livestock |publisher=Cornell College of Agriculture and Life Sciences |access-date=April 30, 2025}}</ref>

===Aerial toxins===
The leaves, stems and flowers of ''Helleborus niger'' contain [[ranunculin]]<ref name="Susan"/> and ranuncoside <ref name="Cuny">{{cite journal |last1=Cuny |first1=Eckehard |title=Bioactive Ingredients of Helleborus niger L. (Christmas Rose): The Renaissance of an Old Medicinal Herb—A Review |journal=Natural Product Communications |date=September 12, 2023 |volume=18 |issue=9 |doi=10.1177/1934578X231201053 |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1934578X231201053?icid=int.sj-full-text.similar-articles.7#bibr22-1934578X231201053 |access-date=April 12, 2025|doi-access=free }}</ref> - glycosides whose breakdown yields the [[toxin]] [[protoanemonin]] when plant cells are damaged.<ref name="Olson">[https://books.google.com/books?id=vuec3nTovyUC&dq=active+poisons+helleborus&pg=PA309 Olson, Kent R., ''Poisoning & Drug Overdose'', p312] at Google Book Search, accessed 12 January 2009</ref> Protoanemonin has an unpleasant taste and can cause irritation of the skin, [[mucosa]] and eyes upon contact. If large amounts are ingested, the toxin can cause itching and blistering of the mouth and throat<ref name="Margit">{{cite journal |last1=Müller |first1=Margit |last2=Bertrams |first2=Julia |last3=Stinting |first3=Florian |title=Stability of protoanemonin in plant extracts from Helleborus niger L. and Pulsatilla vulgaris Mill. |journal=Journal of Pharmaceutical and Biomedical Analysis |date=September 5, 2020 |volume=188 |issue=5 |doi=10.1016/j.jpba.2020.113370 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0731708520312565?via%3Dihub#bib0015 |access-date=April 20, 2025|url-access=subscription }}</ref> as well as [[gastroenteritis]] and [[hematemesis]] in both humans and animals.<ref name="Olson" /><ref name="Bai">{{cite journal |last1=Bai |first1=Yili |last2=Benn |first2=Michael |last3=Majak |first3=Walter |last4=McDiamid |first4=Ruth |title=Extraction and HPLC Determination of Ranunculin in Species of the Buttercup Family |journal=Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry |date=August 15, 1996 |volume=44 |issue=8 |pages=2235-2238 |doi=10.1021/jf950626m |url=https://doi.org/10.1021/jf950626m |access-date=March 28, 2025|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

[[File:Black Hellebore root 001.jpg|thumb|Black Helleborus Root]]

===Root toxins===
A key compound in the roots of ''Helleborus niger'' is Hellebrin, a [[bufadienolide]] which has similar cardiac activity but is less toxic than the [[cardiac glycoside|cardiac glycosides]] found in ''[[Digitalis]]'' and ''[[Strophanthus]]'' plants. The degradation products of Hellebrin also strengthen heart contractions, but are more toxic than their parent molecule. The [[aglycon]] Hellebrigenin has the lowest lethal dose along with stronger cardiac activity than the original [[glucoside]] Hellebrin.<ref name="Cuny"/> Though rare, Hellebrin and its derivatives are considered responsible for severe or lethal Christmas Rose poisonings because their interference with the ion channels of the heart can lead to various [[arrhythmias]].<ref name= "Cornell" />

==Folklore and early medicinal uses==
[[File:Hamburg Museum 1922,21.jpg|thumb|[[Medicinal jar]] with ''Extractum Hellebori nigri'', Hamburg, first half of the 19th century.]]

''Helleborus niger'' is commonly called the [[Christmas]] rose, due to an old legend that it sprouted in the snow from the tears of a young girl who had no gift to give the [[Child Jesus|Christ child]] in [[Bethlehem]].<ref name="RHSD" />

One legend states that the flower blooms at the abbey in England founded by St. Thomas. It is said to bloom near the new calendar date of 6 January.<ref>{{cite web |title=The myth of the Christmas rose |url=https://www.cantsroses.co.uk/the-myth-of-the-christmas-rose/ |website=Cants of Colchester Ltd |access-date=17 November 2022}}</ref> This date had been Christmas Day under the old [[Julian calendar]]. So when Christmas Day under the new calendar came around and the flower did not bloom, it was such a frightful omen that England did not adopt the [[Gregorian calendar]] at that time in 1588; adoption had to wait until 1751.{{Citation needed|date=October 2009}}

In the Middle Ages, people strewed the flowers on the floors of their homes to drive out evil influences.{{Citation needed|date=October 2009}} They blessed their animals with it and used it to ward off the power of witches. These same people believed, however, that witches employed the herb in their spells and that sorcerers tossed the powdered herb into the air around them to make themselves invisible.{{Citation needed|date=October 2009}}

In the early days of medicine, two kinds of hellebore were recognized: '''black hellebore''', which included various species of ''Helleborus'', and '''white hellebore'''<ref name=EB1911>{{Cite EB1911|wstitle=Hellebore |volume=13 |pages=235–236}}</ref> (now known as ''[[Veratrum album]]'' or "false hellebore", which belongs to a different plant family, the [[Melanthiaceae]]).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.mobot.org/MOBOT/Research/APweb/genera/melanthiaceaegen.html|title=Melanthiaceae Genera|website=www.mobot.org}}</ref> Black hellebore was used by the ancients to treat insanity, melancholy, gout and epilepsy.<ref>[[Pliny the Elder|Pliny]], ''[[Natural History (Pliny)|N.H.]]'', XXII.64, XXV.21</ref> It is also toxic, causing [[tinnitus]], [[vertigo (medical)|vertigo]], stupor, thirst, a feeling of suffocation, swelling of the tongue and throat, [[emesis]] and [[catharsis]], [[bradycardia]] (slowing of the [[pulse]]), and finally collapse and death from [[cardiac arrest]].<ref name=EB1911/> Research in the 1970s, however, showed that the roots of ''H. niger'' do not contain the cardiotoxic compounds helleborin, hellebrin, and helleborein that are responsible for the lethal reputation of black hellebore. It seems that earlier studies may have used a commercial preparation containing a mixture of material from other species such as ''[[Helleborus viridis]]'', green hellebore.<ref name="Susan"/>

In antiquity the most famous place for the black hellebore was the Phokian city of [[Anticyra|Antikyra]]<ref>Theophrastus,  HP ΙΧ 10.2-4; Dioscorides, ''De materia medica'' IV 148-152, 162; Plinius, HN XXV. 21</ref> in Greece.

Black hellebore was the dominant purgative of antiquity, frequently prescribed for that purpose by [[Hippocrates]], the father of medicine, in the fifth century B.C. It was said to be introduced by [[Melampus]], with which he healed the madness of the daughters of Proteus, king of Argos.<ref name=EB1911/> The sedative property of hellebore was noted about one hundred years later by [[Theophrastus]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Robison|first1=Victor|title=Victory Over Pain: A History of Anesthia|date=1946|publisher=London Sigma Books|pages=5}}</ref>
